WITNESSES TO A WILL — ATTESTATION, INTERESTED WITNESSES, AND THE HARMLESS-ERROR RULE (PROB. CODE §§ 6104, 6110-6113, 8220-8221, 8252-8253; EVID. CODE §§ 605-606; ESTATE OF SAUERESSIG; ESTATE OF STOKER; ESTATE OF BEN-ALI) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Harold P. Nakamura · Alameda

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about the witnesses to a will: how many witnesses an attested will must have and what each of them must do; who may act as a witness; when the witnesses must sign; what happens when the witnessing formalities were not followed but the testator’s intent can be proved by clear and convincing evidence; what the Probate Code provides when a witness is also given something by the will; how the presumption that arises in that situation operates and what it costs the witness if it is not rebutted; the separate rule that an execution procured by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence is ineffective; the holographic will, which needs no witnesses at all; the alternative ways a written will may be validly executed; and how a will’s execution is proved in the probate court when no one contests it, when no subscribing witness is available, and when due execution is contested. It is prepared as background in connection with the will of Harold P. Nakamura and any proceeding concerning that will in Alameda County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not say whether any particular will was validly executed, who should or should not act as a witness, or what any person should do.

THE WRITING, SIGNATURE, AND TWO-WITNESS REQUIREMENTS (PROB. CODE § 6110(A)-(C)(1))
Chapter 2 of Part 1 of Division 6 of the Probate Code, sections 6110 through 6113, is titled “Execution of Wills.” Section 6110(a) states that, except as provided in that part, a will shall be in writing and satisfy the requirements of the section. Subdivision (b) names three ways the will may be signed: by the testator; in the testator’s name by some other person, in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction; or by a conservator under a court order to make a will under section 2580. Subdivision (c)(1) states the witnessing requirement: the will shall be witnessed by being signed, during the testator’s lifetime, by at least two persons, each of whom (A) being present at the same time, witnessed either the signing of the will or the testator’s acknowledgment of the signature or of the will, and (B) understand that the instrument they sign is the testator’s will. The subdivision therefore asks two things of each of the two witnesses — presence at the same time at the signing or the acknowledgment, and an understanding that the instrument is the testator’s will — and it asks that their signatures be placed on the will during the testator’s lifetime. Whether the will of Harold P. Nakamura meets these requirements is a question this sheet does not answer.

FORMALITIES THE SECTION NO LONGER CONTAINS (ESTATE OF SAUERESSIG)
In Estate of Saueressig the California Supreme Court described what the 1983 revision that produced section 6110 left out of the statute. The opinion states that section 6110 eliminated several technical requirements, including the requirement that the witnesses sign the will in the testator’s presence, and elsewhere lists the other requirements of the former statute that were dropped, among them that the testator’s signature be at the end of the will, that the testator declare to the witnesses that the instrument is his or her will, that the witnesses’ signatures be at the end of the will, and that the testator request the witnesses to sign. The text of section 6110(c)(1) set out in the preceding clause is what the section now requires. What an attested will does not have to contain is a matter of the statute’s text and of the legislative history the opinion recounts; this sheet does not say what any particular will contains.

WHO MAY ACT AS A WITNESS (PROB. CODE § 6112(A))
Section 6112(a) states the qualification for a witness in a single sentence: any person generally competent to be a witness may act as a witness to a will. The subdivision refers to general competency as a witness, a subject governed by the Evidence Code rather than by the Probate Code, and it adds no separate age, residence, relationship, or disinterest requirement of its own. The consequences of a witness also being a person to whom the will makes a gift are addressed in subdivisions (b), (c) and (d) of the same section, which are set out in later clauses of this sheet. Who witnessed the will of Harold P. Nakamura, and whether any of them was generally competent to be a witness, are questions this sheet does not answer.

SIGNING DURING THE TESTATOR’S LIFETIME (PROB. CODE § 6110(C)(1); ESTATE OF SAUERESSIG)
The words “during the testator’s lifetime” appear in section 6110(c)(1) as the section now reads; the section carries the credit line “Amended by Stats. 2008, Ch. 53, Sec. 1. Effective January 1, 2009.” Before that amendment the subdivision contained no express words about when the witnesses had to sign, and in 2006 the California Supreme Court decided in Estate of Saueressig what the earlier text meant. The court held that the signature of a witness affixed after the testator’s death does not satisfy the statute, describing such postdeath subscription as not permitted. The opinion gives the court’s reasons: a rule allowing postdeath attestation would substitute oral testimony for the Legislature’s requirement of a written signature, would encourage will contests, and would put witnesses rather than the testator in control of the disposition of an estate; and the court concluded that, given the history and context of the subdivision, postdeath attestation is not an act the Legislature has authorized. When the witnesses to the will of Harold P. Nakamura signed is a question this sheet does not answer.

A WILL NOT EXECUTED IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE WITNESSING REQUIREMENT (PROB. CODE § 6110(C)(2); ESTATE OF BEN-ALI)
Section 6110(c)(2) supplies an alternative to compliance with paragraph (1). If a will was not executed in compliance with paragraph (1), the will shall be treated as if it was executed in compliance with that paragraph if the proponent of the will establishes by clear and convincing evidence that, at the time the testator signed the will, the testator intended the will to constitute the testator’s will. The paragraph places the burden on the proponent, fixes the time the intent must have existed as the time the testator signed, and sets the standard of proof at clear and convincing evidence rather than the preponderance standard ordinarily used in civil matters. In Estate of Ben-Ali the Court of Appeal described the paragraph in the same terms and then held, on the record before it, that no reasonable trier of fact could find the standard had been reached, reversing a judgment that had admitted the will to probate. Whether the paragraph would apply to the will of Harold P. Nakamura, and what evidence would satisfy it, are questions this sheet does not answer.

THE REACH OF THE HARMLESS-ERROR PARAGRAPH (ESTATE OF STOKER)
In Estate of Stoker the Court of Appeal considered a will that was handwritten but not holographic and that bore no witness signatures at all, and addressed two arguments about the scope of section 6110(c)(2). On the first, the court said the statute contains no language indicating that the wills it covers are limited to typewritten wills, and that handwritten nonholographic wills are therefore not excluded from the scope of the statute. On the second, the court rejected the argument that a paragraph effective January 1, 2009 could not be applied to a document signed in 2005, observing that the paragraph governs the procedure and evidentiary standard probate courts must currently use in conducting trials on the validity of wills. The case was tried in 2009. Whether the reasoning of that decision would reach any document connected with Harold P. Nakamura is a question this sheet does not answer.

A WILL SIGNED BY AN INTERESTED WITNESS IS NOT INVALID FOR THAT REASON (PROB. CODE § 6112(B))
Section 6112(b) states that a will, or any provision of it, is not invalid because the will is signed by an interested witness. The subdivision addresses the validity of the instrument and of its provisions; it does not by itself decide what the interested witness receives, which is the subject of subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same section. The Probate Code does not define “interested witness” in this section; subdivision (c) speaks instead of a will that “makes a devise to a subscribing witness.” Whether any witness to the will of Harold P. Nakamura is a person to whom the will makes a devise is a question this sheet does not answer.

THE PRESUMPTION RAISED BY A DEVISE TO A SUBSCRIBING WITNESS (PROB. CODE § 6112(C); EVID. CODE §§ 605, 606)
Section 6112(c) attaches a presumption to a devise made by the will to a subscribing witness. Unless there are at least two other subscribing witnesses to the will who are disinterested witnesses, the fact that the will makes a devise to a subscribing witness creates a presumption that the witness procured the devise by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence. The subdivision says the presumption is a presumption affecting the burden of proof, and it states one exception: the presumption does not apply where the witness is a person to whom the devise is made solely in a fiduciary capacity. The Evidence Code supplies the meaning of the classification the subdivision uses. Section 605 of that code describes a presumption affecting the burden of proof as one established to implement some public policy other than to facilitate the determination of the particular action, and section 606 states its effect: it imposes upon the party against whom it operates the burden of proof as to the nonexistence of the presumed fact. Whether the will of Harold P. Nakamura makes a devise to a subscribing witness, and whether there are two other subscribing witnesses who are disinterested, are questions this sheet does not answer.

WHAT THE INTERESTED WITNESS TAKES IF THE PRESUMPTION IS NOT REBUTTED (PROB. CODE § 6112(D))
Section 6112(d) states what happens when the presumption applies to a devise and the witness fails to rebut it. In that situation the devise fails, and the interested witness shall take such proportion of the devise made to the witness in the will as does not exceed the share of the estate which would be distributed to the witness if the will were not established. The measure is therefore the witness’s share had the will not been established, used as a ceiling on what the witness may take under the devise; a witness who would take nothing in the absence of the will takes nothing under this subdivision. The subdivision closes with a saving sentence: nothing in it affects the law that applies where it is established that the witness procured a devise by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence. What, if anything, any witness to the will of Harold P. Nakamura would take is a question this sheet does not answer.

EXECUTION PROCURED BY DURESS, MENACE, FRAUD, OR UNDUE INFLUENCE (PROB. CODE § 6104)
Section 6104 states a rule that applies to the execution of a will whoever the witnesses are: the execution or revocation of a will or a part of a will is ineffective to the extent the execution or revocation was procured by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence. The section speaks of ineffectiveness “to the extent” of the procurement, so it reaches a part of a will as well as the whole. The same four grounds appear in the presumption in section 6112(c) and in the saving sentence of section 6112(d), which preserves the law that applies where procurement by those means is established. Chapter 2 of Part 1 of Division 6 of the Probate Code, sections 6110 through 6113, is titled “Execution of Wills.” Section 6110(a) states that, except as provided in that part, a will shall be in writing and satisfy the requirements of the section. expectedJSON.body: Estate of Ben-Ali addressed what a probate court may presume about due execution from the face of a will. The Court of Appeal read the leading Supreme Court decision on the subject, Estate of Pitcairn (1936) 6 Cal.2d 730, as holding not that a regular and complete attestation clause establishes the genuineness of an unknown signature, but the converse — that proof of the genuineness of the subscribing witnesses’ signatures is sufficient to create a presumption of due execution notwithstanding an irregular or incomplete attestation clause. The court summarized the rule this way: proof of the signatures of the decedent and the witnesses makes out a prima facie case of due execution, and proof of the signature of the decedent and of only one of the witnesses does not. In the case before it, the signature of the second witness was indecipherable and unauthenticated, and the court held the will could not be admitted on the basis of section 6110(c)(1). Whether the signatures on the will of Harold P. Nakamura could be shown to be genuine is a question this sheet does not answer.
